claim: Voltage-gated sodium channels are targets for a range of pharmaceutical drugs developed for the treatment of neurological diseases.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channels are targets for a range of pharmaceutical drugs developed for the treatment of neurological diseases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Cannabidiol (CBD) was recently approved for treatment of two types of epilepsy associated with sodium channel mutations.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), the non-psychoactive compound isolated from cannabis plants, was recently approved for treatment of two types of epilepsy associated with sodium channel mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract, referring to regulatory approval.

claim: CBD binds at a novel site at the interface of the fenestrations and the central hydrophobic cavity of the NavMs channel.
source: CBD binds at a novel site at the interface of the fenestrations and the central hydrophobic cavity of the channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by the crystal structure data presented in the study.

claim: CBD binding at the fenestration-cavity interface blocks the transmembrane-spanning sodium ion translocation pathway.
source: Binding at this site blocks the transmembrane-spanning sodium ion translocation pathway, providing a molecular mechanism for channel inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing CBD location and HOLE analysis demonstrating pore blockage.

claim: Nine homologous human sodium channel subtypes (hNav1.1-hNav1.9) have been identified with different functional characteristics and expression profiles.
source: Nine homologous human sodium channel subtypes, designated hNav1.1-hNav1.9 have been identified, which have different functional characteristics and expression profiles within different tissues (Catterall et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from prior literature (Catterall et al., 2005).

claim: Mutations in hNavs have been associated with a range of channelopathies, including pain, epilepsy, and heart disorders.
source: Mutations in hNavs have been associated with a range of channelopathies, including pain, epilepsy, and heart disorders, making them major targets for drug development (Bagal et al., 2015; Kaplan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: THC has been primarily associated with psychoactive drug use.
source: Whilst THC has been primarily associated with psychoactive drug use (Rosenberg et al., 2015; Pisanti et al., 2017), the non-psychoactive component, CBD, has been shown to have clinical applications as a therapeutic drug for treatment of epileptic conditions (Rosenberg et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CBD has been shown to have clinical applications as a therapeutic drug for treatment of epileptic conditions.
source: the non-psychoactive component, CBD, has been shown to have clinical applications as a therapeutic drug for treatment of epileptic conditions (Rosenberg et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CBD was recently approved by the European Medicines Agency and the Federal Drug Administration for use in children for treatment of Dravet Syndrome and Lenox-Gastaut Syndrome.
source: and was recently approved by the European Medicines Agency and the Federal Drug Administration for use in children for treatment of Dravet Syndrome and Lenox-Gastaut Syndrome (Sarker and Nahar, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature documenting regulatory approval.

claim: Dravet Syndrome and Lenox-Gastaut Syndrome are rare early-onset epilepsies associated with Navs.
source: Both of these diseases are rare early-onset epilepsies associated with Navs, with Dravet patients often having mutations in the hNav1.1 gene SCN1A (Marini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Dravet patients often have mutations in the hNav1.1 gene SCN1A.
source: with Dravet patients often having mutations in the hNav1.1 gene SCN1A (Marini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The molecular basis of CBD's target interactions with ion channels and receptors remains unclear.
source: Despite a significant amount of evidence reporting on the effectiveness of CBD for treating epileptic conditions (Cross et al., 2017; Devinsky et al., 2018), the molecular basis of its target interactions with ion channels and receptors still remains unclear (Watkins, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: CBD both blocks the pore and stabilizes the inactivated states of sodium channels.
source: Functional studies have suggested that CBD both blocks the pore and stabilizes the inactivated states of sodium channels.
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies referenced in the text.

claim: CBD inhibits the channel activities of human Nav1.1-Nav1.7 isoforms and NaChBac with IC50s ranging from 1.5 to 3.8 µM.
source: It inhibits the channel activities of human Nav1.1-Nav1.7 isoforms, as well as those of the prokaryotic Nav homologue NaChBac, with IC50s ranging from 1.5 to 3.8 µM, suggesting inhibition occurs at physiologically-relevant concentrations (Patel et al., 2016; Ghovanloo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: CBD preference for the inactivated state is a characteristic of classic pore blockers.
source: This preference for the inactivated state is a characteristic of classic pore blockers (Kuo and Bean, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The resurgent and persistent sodium currents of hNav1.2 have been shown to be inhibited at CBD concentrations of 1 µM.
source: Furthermore the resurgent and persistent sodium currents of hNav1.2 have been shown to be inhibited at CBD concentrations of 1 µM (Mason and Cummins, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The structural basis of the interactions of CBD and Navs has not been identified on a molecular level prior to this study.
source: However, to date, the structural basis of the interactions of CBD and Navs has not been identified on a molecular level.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: NavMs exhibits highly similar functional characteristics to hNavs.
source: The NavMs channel has been shown to be an excellent exemplar for hNavs as it exhibits highly similar functional (Bagnéris et al., 2014; Ke et al., 2018), conductance (Ulmschneider et al., 2013), and drug-binding (similar IC50 values) characteristics (Bagnéris et al., 2014), as well as sequence and structural homologies (Sula et al., 2017; Sula and Wallace, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: NavMs exhibits highly similar conductance characteristics to hNavs.
source: The NavMs channel has been shown to be an excellent exemplar for hNavs as it exhibits highly similar functional (Bagnéris et al., 2014; Ke et al., 2018), conductance (Ulmschneider et al., 2013), and drug-binding (similar IC50 values) characteristics (Bagnéris et al., 2014), as well as sequence and structural homologies (Sula et al., 2017; Sula and Wallace, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: NavMs exhibits similar drug-binding characteristics (similar IC50 values) to hNavs.
source: The NavMs channel has been shown to be an excellent exemplar for hNavs as it exhibits highly similar functional (Bagnéris et al., 2014; Ke et al., 2018), conductance (Ulmschneider et al., 2013), and drug-binding (similar IC50 values) characteristics (Bagnéris et al., 2014), as well as sequence and structural homologies (Sula et al., 2017; Sula and Wallace, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: NavMs exhibits sequence and structural homologies to hNavs.
source: The NavMs channel has been shown to be an excellent exemplar for hNavs as it exhibits highly similar functional (Bagnéris et al., 2014; Ke et al., 2018), conductance (Ulmschneider et al., 2013), and drug-binding (similar IC50 values) characteristics (Bagnéris et al., 2014), as well as sequence and structural homologies (Sula et al., 2017; Sula and Wallace, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: NavMs channels are tetramers with each monomer consisting of six transmembrane helices.
source: NavMs channels are tetramers with each monomer consisting of six transmembrane (TM) helices (4 of which form each of the voltage sensor subdomains and 2 of which form the pore subdomains)
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about NavMs.

claim: All hNav channel isoforms are monomers of four similar but not identical domains.
source: whilst all of the hNav channel isoforms are monomers of four similar but not identical domains (each of which also consists of 6 transmembrane helices that are comprised of 4-helical voltage sensor subdomains and 2-helical pore subdomains) plus inter-domain loop regions (which differ considerably between hNavs, but are not involved in the CBD-binding sites).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about hNavs.

claim: Crystal structures of NavMs provide the highest resolution (~2.2–2.5 Å) views of any sodium channel to date.
source: The compelling reason for using crystal structures of NavMs in this study is that they provide the, to date, highest resolution (~2.2–2.5 Å) views of any sodium channel (Naylor et al., 2016; Sula et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: NavMs has strong sequence, structural and functional similarities to hNav1.1 and hNav1.2 channels.
source: This, combined with its strong sequence, structural and functional similarities (Sula et al., 2017; Sula and Wallace, 2017) to hNav1.1 and hNav1.2 channels, enables important comparisons with sodium channels found in human brain tissues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of hNavs available to date generally have overall resolutions of ~4–5 Å.
source: Furthermore the cryo-EM structures of hNavs available to date generally have overall resolutions of ~4–5 Å, with the transmembrane regions having the best resolutions of ~3 Å (not sufficient for detailed views of the binding sites)
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about the state of hNav structural biology.

claim: NavMs and hNav1.1 exhibit similar ion flux and other conductance properties.
source: but NavMs and hNav1.1 have been shown to exhibit similar ion flux and other conductance properties, as well as very similar binding affinities for a wide range of sodium channel-specific drugs (Bagnéris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: NavMs and hNav1.1 have very similar binding affinities for a wide range of sodium channel-specific drugs.
source: but NavMs and hNav1.1 have been shown to exhibit similar ion flux and other conductance properties, as well as very similar binding affinities for a wide range of sodium channel-specific drugs (Bagnéris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The CBD-binding site is located in the hydrophobic pockets present between subunits that run perpendicular to the channel direction.
source: The CBD-binding site is located and clearly visible (Figure 1 and 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) in a well-defined region of the NavMs-CBD structure, sited in the hydrophobic pockets present between subunits that run perpendicular to the channel direction (Montini et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in figures and cited literature about fenestrations.

claim: Fenestrations are located in the transmembrane region, just below the level of the selectivity filter.
source: (such features have been designated 'fenestrations' and are located (horizontally in Figure 1) in the transmembrane region, just below the level of the selectivity filter), and are the features originally proposed by Hille, 1977 as sites for ingress of hydrophobic drugs into the channel interior.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and citation to Hille's original proposal.

claim: Fenestrations were originally proposed by Hille, 1977 as sites for ingress of hydrophobic drugs into the channel interior.
source: and are the features originally proposed by Hille, 1977 as sites for ingress of hydrophobic drugs into the channel interior.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hille's work.

claim: CBD is located at the ends of the fenestrations that lie closest to the central pore, and protrudes into the central transmembrane cavity.
source: CBD is located at the ends of the fenestrations that lie closest to the central pore, and protrudes into (and blocks) the central transmembrane cavity, just below the sodium ion selectivity filter (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is experimental electron density and enough room for four CBD molecules in the NavMs channel.
source: There is experimental electron density (Figure 2A, right panel) and enough room (Figure 2A, third panel from left) for four CBD molecules in this region
evidence: This is supported by the electron density maps shown in Figure 2A.

claim: One CBD molecule would be sufficient to block sodium ion passage through NavMs.
source: although one would be sufficient to block sodium ion passage, as seen from the HOLE (Smart et al., 1993) depictions (Figure 2B) and pore radius plots (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by HOLE analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Each CBD binding site is comprised of 11 residues from three different subunits in NavMs.
source: Each binding site is comprised of 11 residues from three different subunits in NavMs (shown in detail and in different colours in Figure 1D & E).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1D & E.

claim: The corresponding residues to the NavMs CBD-binding site in hNavs arise from three different domains of the same polypeptide chain.
source: The corresponding residues in hNavs arise from three different domains of the same polypeptide chain (Figure 3).
evidence: This is inferred from structural alignment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The apo structure of NavMs also exhibits some electron density in the CBD-binding region, which has been attributed to detergent molecules.
source: It should be noted here, that this region of the apo structure also exhibits some electron density (but has a different size and shape), which has been attributed to detergent molecules.
evidence: This is based on interpretation of electron density in the apo structure.

claim: The (2Fo-Fc) electron density map of the CBD complex clearly indicates that in these crystals the site is occupied by CBD rather than by detergent.
source: The (2Fo-Fc) electron density map of the CBD complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) clearly indicates that in these crystals the site is occupied by CBD rather than by detergent.
evidence: This is supported by the electron density map shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The location of the CBD-binding site is very close to the locations of the binding sites for analgesic and other hydrophobic compounds in NavMs.
source: The location of the CBD-binding site is very close to the locations of the binding sites that have been identified for analgesic and other hydrophobic compounds in NavMs (Bagnéris et al., 2014; Figure 4) as well as in another bacterial sodium channel, NavAb (Gamal El-Din et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 4 and citations to prior studies.

claim: All of the interactions between CBD and NavMs except one involve hydrophobic interactions rather than hydrogen-bond formation.
source: All of the interactions seen except one, that of residue M175 (Figure 1E), involve hydrophobic interactions rather than hydrogen-bond formation
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The interaction between the main chain carbonyl of residue M175 and the OH group present in CBD may be important for specificity of binding.
source: (but that particular interaction between the main chain carbonyl of residue M175 and the OH group present in CBD, may be important for specificity of binding – see below).
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural observation and later discussion about THC.

claim: CBD inhibits NavMs less potently than other Nav channels previously studied.
source: In the present study it was shown that CBD inhibits NavMs less potently and with a slightly shallower Hill slope than the other Nav channels previously studied (Ghovanloo et al., 2018 Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CBD inhibits NavMs with a slightly shallower Hill slope than other Nav channels previously studied.
source: In the present study it was shown that CBD inhibits NavMs less potently and with a slightly shallower Hill slope than the other Nav channels previously studied (Ghovanloo et al., 2018 Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The moderate variation in CBD inhibition potency between human Navs and NavMs is consistent with previous reports using other Nav blockers.
source: The moderate variation in CBD inhibition potency between human Navs and NavMs is consistent with previous reports using other Nav blockers (Bagnéris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: CBD inhibits NavMs similarly to other Nav channels.
source: Overall, these results show that CBD inhibits NavMs similarly to other Nav channels and, thus supports the proposed interaction inside the pore depicted in the NavMs structure as being functionally relevant.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology results and comparison with prior studies.

claim: The IC50 for CBD inhibition of wild-type NavMs is 17.8 ± 0.5 µM with a Hill slope of 1.5 ± 0.1.
source: The IC50 for CBD inhibition of wild-type NavMs is 17.8 ± 0.5 µM with a Hill slope of 1.5 ± 0.1 (the S.E. values quoted are errors of the fit, n = 8 panel-wide).
evidence: This is directly measured from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Residue T207 in NavMs is located in the CBD-binding site with its side chain involved in hydrophobic interactions with the drug.
source: This residue is located in the CBD-binding site (Figure 1E), with its side chain involved in hydrophobic interactions with the drug.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Threonine T207 has the closest sidechain (3.7 Å) to the CBD molecule in NavMs.
source: This threonine has the closest sidechain (3.7 Å) to the CBD molecule.
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure.

claim: The mutation of T207 to alanine results in a modest reduction in CBD block of NavMs.
source: The mutation of the threonine side chain to a smaller alanine side chain results in a modest reduction in the CBD block (Figure 5B,C), hence correlating its location with a functional effect.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: T207 in NavMs is well established as a primary binding site for local anaesthetics.
source: In NavMs, the involvement of the T207 residue is of importance as it is well established as a primary binding site for local anaesthetics (and has been shown to be involved in the electrophysiology studies on NavMs reported herein).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by the electrophysiology data in this study.

claim: When the equivalent residue (F1774) to T207 was mutated in hNav1.1, the binding affinity of CBD decreased by a factor of ~2.5.
source: Furthermore, when the equivalent residue (F1774) was mutated in hNav1.1 (boxed in Figure 6), the binding affinity of CBD was found to decrease by a factor of ~2.5 (Ghovanloo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: CBD and THC have previously been shown to inhibit hNav1.2 with similar potencies.
source: CBD and THC have previously been shown to inhibit hNav1.2 with similar potencies, however the THC inhibition slope was less steep than that of CBD (Ghovanloo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The THC inhibition slope on hNav1.2 was less steep than that of CBD.
source: CBD and THC have previously been shown to inhibit hNav1.2 with similar potencies, however the THC inhibition slope was less steep than that of CBD (Ghovanloo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The chemical structures of CBD and THC differ only by the presence of an additional free hydroxyl group on one of the rings in CBD.
source: The chemical structures of CBD and THC are very similar (Figure 7A), differing only by the presence of an additional free hydroxyl group on one of the rings in CBD (in THC the equivalent oxygen forms part of a closed pyran ring).
evidence: This is based on the known chemical structures shown in Figure 7A.

claim: THC can be physically and sterically accommodated in the CBD-binding site with the same orientation as CBD.
source: As can be seen in Figure 7B, by placing the THC structure into the CBD-binding site with the same orientation as found for CBD, it can be physically and sterically accommodated.
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 7B.

claim: THC is missing the hydrogen bond between the oxygen of the main chain residue M175 and the drug that is present in the CBD-NavMs complex.
source: However, and crucially, it is missing the one electrostatic interaction seen between CBD and NavMs: the hydrogen bond between the oxygen of the main chain residue M175 and the drug (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and modeling shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The absence of the additional free hydroxyl group in THC accounts for the missing hydrogen bond in the THC-protein complex.
source: This is the consequence of the absence of the additional free hydroxyl group in THC, as noted above. That hydroxyl group is the one which forms the hydrogen bond present in the CBD-protein complex
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and chemical differences between CBD and THC.

claim: The additional hydroxyl group in CBD provides an additional intermolecular interaction that could account for the differences in functional effects (inhibition slopes) of CBD and THC on voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: and provides an additional intermolecular interaction for CBD, which could account for the differences in functional effects (inhibition slopes) of the two compounds on voltage-gated sodium channels.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural differences and known functional differences.

claim: CBD has been suggested to be a potential activator of the TRPV2 channel.
source: CBD has also been suggested to be a potential activator of the Transient Receptor Potential Cation Channel Subfamily V Member 2 (TRPV2) channel (Qin et al., 2008; Morelli et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: TRPV2 is a channel which facilitates the non-specific movement of both sodium and calcium ions through plasma membranes.
source: a channel which facilitates the non-specific movement of both sodium and calcium ions through plasma membranes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TRPV2.

claim: CBD activates rat TRPV2 with an EC50 of 3.7 µM according to electrophysiology studies.
source: According to electrophysiology studies, CBD activates rat TRPV2 with an EC50 of 3.7 µM (Qin et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental study.

claim: The link between TRPV2 and epilepsy is much less direct than that for sodium channels.
source: although the link with epilepsy (Morelli et al., 2013) is much less direct than that for sodium channels.
evidence: This is stated as an assessment based on cited literature.

claim: Cryo-EM was used to elucidate the structure of TRPV2 in a CBD-bound state at a nominal resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: Recently cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) was used to elucidate the structure of TRPV2 in a CBD-bound state at a nominal resolution of 3.2 Å (Pumroy et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural study.

claim: The TRPV2 cryo-EM study indicated the presence of CBD in the pore region of the protein.
source: that study indicated the presence of CBD in the pore region of the protein, thus supporting the proposal for TRPV2 being a candidate target for CBD binding.
evidence: This is based on the cited cryo-EM study.

claim: The lower resolution of the TRPV2 structure did not allow detailed analysis of the CBD binding site.
source: The general location of the CBD was visible in the structure, although the lower resolution of that structure did not allow detailed analysis of its binding site.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of the cited TRPV2 structure.

claim: CBD interactions in TRPV2 appear to involve a number of hydrophobic side chains.
source: However, its interactions appear to involve a number of hydrophobic side chains, whilst requiring a partial refolding of the adjacent region of the protein polypeptide.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cited TRPV2 structure.

claim: CBD binding to TRPV2 requires a partial refolding of the adjacent region of the protein polypeptide.
source: However, its interactions appear to involve a number of hydrophobic side chains, whilst requiring a partial refolding of the adjacent region of the protein polypeptide.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cited TRPV2 structure.

claim: The binding site for CBD in TRPV2 is in a similar region to that of CBD in NavMs.
source: The binding site found for CBD in the TRPV2 structure is in a similar region to that of CBD in NavMs (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 8.

claim: The sodium channel-CBD site is located further into the fenestration than it is in TRPV2.
source: However, the sodium channel-CBD site is located further into the fenestration than it is in TRPV2, but closer to the ion binding sites
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 8.

claim: The sodium channel-CBD site is closer to the ion binding sites than the TRPV2-CBD site.
source: However, the sodium channel-CBD site is located further into the fenestration than it is in TRPV2, but closer to the ion binding sites
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The location of the CBD-binding site in sodium channels could more effectively modulate effects in the transmembrane passageway for ion conductance compared to TRPV2.
source: and thus could more effectively modulate effects in the transmembrane passageway for ion conductance, and could account for sodium channels being blocked by CBD, whilst TRPV2 channels appear to be activated by them (Morelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural differences and known functional differences.

claim: Sodium channels are blocked by CBD whilst TRPV2 channels appear to be activated by CBD.
source: and could account for sodium channels being blocked by CBD, whilst TRPV2 channels appear to be activated by them (Morelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on prior functional studies and the data in this manuscript.

claim: CBD-binding blocks the transmembrane pathway for sodium ion translocation through the membrane.
source: This study has demonstrated the nature of the interactions of CBD and a voltage-gated sodium channel, showing that CBD-binding blocks the transmembrane pathway for sodium ion translocation through the membrane (Naylor et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and HOLE analysis in this study.

claim: CBD-binding provides a potential mechanism for the functioning of CBD in sodium channels.
source: and hence provides a potential mechanism for the functioning of CBD in sodium channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The study suggests a possible molecular basis for the medicinal effects of CBD in the treatment of epilepsies.
source: It further suggests a possible molecular basis for the medicinal effects of CBD in the treatment of epilepsies, as sodium channels have been shown to be causally-related to various types of human epilepsy, with disease-related mutations interfering with sodium ion transmembrane flux.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural findings and known links between sodium channels and epilepsy.

claim: Sodium channels have been shown to be causally-related to various types of human epilepsy.
source: as sodium channels have been shown to be causally-related to various types of human epilepsy, with disease-related mutations interfering with sodium ion transmembrane flux.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The CBD-binding site is a novel site, near to, but not coincident with, known analgesic binding sites in sodium channels.
source: The CBD-binding site is a novel site, near to, but not coincident with, known analgesic binding sites in sodium channels.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with known drug binding sites.

claim: The binding site location at the pore end of the transmembrane fenestrations may provide the pathway for CBD to enter and block the channels.
source: The binding site is located at the pore end of the transmembrane fenestrations which enable the ingress of hydrophobic molecules into the channel lumen, hence this may also provide the pathway for CBD to enter and block the channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural location and known function of fenestrations.

claim: The crystal structure of the NavMs-CBD complex was determined at 2.3 Å resolution.
source: The crystal structure (2.3 Å resolution) of the NavMs sodium channel (in coral coloured ribbon depiction) with one CBD molecule (in green space-filing depiction)
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and methods.

claim: The RMSD of the aligned structures of NavMs-CBD and hNav1.2 is 3.2 Å.
source: Structural alignment of the NavMs-CBD crystal structure (coral) and the hNav1.2 cryo-EM structure (grey). The RMSD of the aligned structures is 3.2 Å.
evidence: This is calculated from structural alignment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The RMSD of the alignment between NavMs and TRPV2 structures is 4.2 Å.
source: The RMSD of the alignment is 4.2 Å.
evidence: This is calculated from structural alignment shown in Figure 8.

claim: The best NavMs-CBD crystals were grown at 4°C via the sitting drop vapour diffusion method.
source: The best crystals were grown at 4°C via the sitting drop vapour diffusion method using a 2:1 ratio of the protein and reservoir solutions containing 0.1 M sodium chloride, 0.1M lithium sulphate, 0.1 M HEPES, pH 7, and 30% v/v PEG300.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Data were collected on beamlines at DESY, Soleil Synchrotron, and Diamond Light Source.
source: Data were collected on beamline P13 at the Electron Synchrotron (DESY, Germany); on beamline Proxima1 at the Soleil Synchrotron (France), and on beamlines IO3, IO4, and I24 at the Diamond Light Source (UK).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: Hundreds of crystals were screened and full data sets were collected from more than 40 crystals.
source: Hundreds of crystals were screened and full data sets were collected from more than 40 crystals.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: The structure was determined from crystals which diffracted to 2.2 Å for the apo protein and 2.3 Å for the CBD complex.
source: The structure was determined from the crystals which diffracted to the highest resolution (2.2 Å for the apo protein, and 2.3 Å for the CBD complex).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section.

claim: 100% of the residues in the NavMs-CBD structure were in allowed conformations according to structure quality checks.
source: The structure quality was checked using PROCHECK (Laskowski et al., 1993) and MolProbity (Chen et al., 2010), which indicated that 100% of the residues were in allowed conformations.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section based on validation software.
